claims.text: In-situ TEM or XRD can be used to characterize deformation dynamics in high-entropy alloys.
In-situ characterization will improve understanding of relationships between microstructural evolution and mechanical properties.
The resulting understanding will enable the design of alloys with optimized combinations of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance.
The proposed method applies to as-cast or wrought high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method applies from ambient to elevated temperatures and over various strain rates.
Deformation produces microstructural evolution that includes phase transformations and defect formation.
Deformation-induced planar defects can influence void growth and delay void coalescence.
Deformation-induced microstructural changes lead to improved strength, ductility, and fracture resistance.
The intervention will improve the combination of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to current state-of-the-art high-entropy alloys.
Current state-of-the-art high-entropy alloys have limited understanding of their deformation mechanisms.
Ex-situ characterization may fail to capture dynamic deformation processes.
The exact relationships among microstructural evolution, strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance are not fully understood.
In-situ TEM or XRD followed by mechanical-property testing can evaluate the hypothesis.
Failure to observe significant improvements in all four targeted mechanical properties would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experiment only characterize and test existing alloys, with no alloy-selection, processing, or redesign step, yet the predicted outcome and falsification rule expect the characterization itself to produce improved mechanical properties.
